items.title: The Midterm Turnout Puzzle: Who Actually Votes When the White House Isn't on the Ballot
items.body:
Every four years, American politics seems to take over everything. Campaign ads, debates, and dinner-table arguments all revolve around one race. Two years later, the energy fades. The offices at stake are still important: all 435 House seats, about a third of the Senate, dozens of governorships, and thousands of state legislative seats. Yet far fewer people turn out to choose them.

This gap between presidential and midterm participation is one of the most reliable patterns in U.S. elections. It also shapes which candidates win, which issues get attention, and how each party plans its campaigns.

## How Big Is the Gap?

In recent decades, turnout in midterm elections has usually run well below turnout in presidential years. Typically, somewhere around 40 to 50 percent of eligible voters cast ballots in a midterm, compared with roughly 55 to 66 percent in a presidential election.

The 2018 and 2022 midterms were notable exceptions to the long-running trend of low participation. Both drew historically high turnout for a midterm, with 2018 reaching about 50 percent of eligible voters, the highest rate in roughly a century. Even so, those elections still fell short of the presidential contests that bracketed them. The "drop-off" between presidential and midterm years has narrowed in some cases, but it has not disappeared.

## Who Shows Up

Midterm electorates are not just smaller versions of presidential electorates. They differ in composition.

**Older voters are overrepresented.** Voting rates rise steadily with age. Adults over 65 vote at much higher rates than adults under 30 in every election, but the difference widens in midterm years. In a presidential year, a surge of younger and first-time voters partly offsets this imbalance. In a midterm, that surge is smaller.

**Habitual and partisan voters dominate.** People who vote in every election, including low-profile ones, tend to be more politically engaged and more strongly attached to a party. Occasional voters, who often decide to participate only when a presidential race raises the stakes, are more likely to sit out.

**Education and income matter.** Voters with college degrees and higher household incomes participate at higher rates than others, and these differences also grow in midterm years. Homeowners and people who have lived in the same community for a long time are likewise more likely to vote than renters and recent movers.

## Who Stays Home

The people most likely to skip a midterm include younger adults, newly registered voters, those with lower incomes, and those with less connection to local community institutions. Surveys regularly find several reasons:

- **Low awareness.** Many people simply don't know a midterm is happening, or know little about the candidates on the ballot.
- **Practical barriers.** Work schedules, caregiving duties, transportation, and registration deadlines can all make voting harder, especially when it feels less urgent.
- **Lower perceived stakes.** Without a presidential contest, some people feel their vote matters less, even though many of the decisions that most directly affect daily life are made by state and local officials.
- **Disillusionment.** Some non-voters say they feel neither party speaks to them.

## Why the Gap Matters Politically

Because the midterm electorate is older, more engaged, and more partisan, campaign strategy changes. Candidates and party organizations focus less on persuading undecided voters and more on motivating their committed supporters to show up. A party whose supporters are enthusiastic can benefit from a strong turnout of its base even if its overall support is no larger than the other side's.

The president's party also has a well-documented disadvantage. In most midterm elections since the end of World War II, the party holding the White House has lost seats in the House of Representatives. Political scientists offer several explanations: voters who are dissatisfied with the current administration may be more motivated to vote than those who are content, and the presidential "coattails" that help candidates in a presidential year are absent.

Turnout is not the only factor. Economic conditions, the president's approval rating, redistricting, candidate quality, and the national mood all play major roles. Studies have also found that high turnout does not always favor one party. The effect depends on which groups are mobilized in a given year and place.

## Closing the Gap

Election administrators, civic groups, and campaigns have tried many approaches to boost participation in off-year elections:

- Early voting, mail voting, and extended hours to give voters more flexibility
- Automatic or same-day voter registration in some states
- Nonpartisan outreach that explains what offices are on the ballot and what they do
- Reminders and community-based efforts to reach first-time and infrequent voters

Research suggests that simple, personal contact, such as a neighbor or volunteer encouraging someone to vote, can make a measurable difference. The effects are modest per person, but they add up in close races.

## The Takeaway

The midterm turnout puzzle comes down to a basic fact: the people who decide midterm elections are not a perfect mirror of the country. Those who vote are older, more partisan, and more consistently engaged than those who don't. That reality affects campaign messaging, party fortunes, and ultimately the policies that follow.

For voters, the lesson is simple. Elections with lower turnout give each individual ballot more weight. For anyone curious about how their community is represented, checking registration status, learning what's on the ballot, and making a plan to vote are practical first steps. Election dates, polling places, and deadlines can be confirmed through your state or local election office.

*This article is for general informational purposes and does not endorse any candidate or party. Turnout figures are approximate and vary by source and year.*

items.title: Clocks Fall Back November 1: Why America Still Can't Agree to Stop Changing Time
items.body:
In the early hours of **Sunday, November 1**, most of the United States will turn its clocks back one hour and return to standard time. Many people will enjoy an extra hour of sleep. Many will also be asking a familiar question: why are we still doing this?

Efforts to end the twice-a-year clock change have drawn support from both parties, from the White House and from large parts of the public. Legislation to make daylight saving time permanent has stalled in Congress again. Here is where the debate stands, what research says, and why states can't simply settle the matter themselves.

## How the current system works

The Uniform Time Act of 1966 created a national framework for daylight saving time (DST). Under today's rules, DST runs from the second Sunday in March to the first Sunday in November.

States have limited choices under that law:

- **They can stay on standard time all year.** Hawaii and most of Arizona do this, along with several U.S. territories.
- **They cannot adopt permanent daylight saving time on their own.** That change requires an act of Congress.

Roughly twenty states have passed laws or resolutions that would adopt year-round daylight saving time if Congress permits it. Those measures sit idle until federal law changes.

## Why the push has stalled

The best-known proposal is the Sunshine Protection Act, which would lock in daylight time year-round. The Senate passed a version by unanimous consent in 2022, but it never received a vote in the House. Versions have been reintroduced in later sessions, and public statements of support from political leaders have followed. Still, no bill has reached the president's desk.

Several things keep the issue stuck:

1. **Disagreement over which time to make permanent.** Supporters of permanent daylight time want long summer-style evenings all year. Many sleep scientists argue permanent *standard* time is the better choice. Those two camps split the reform coalition.
2. **Regional differences.** Sunrise and sunset times vary widely across the country. Permanent daylight time would mean very late winter sunrises in some northern and western areas of a time zone.
3. **Limited floor time.** Congress has many competing priorities, and a change that touches every clock in the country is easy to postpone.

## What the sleep evidence says

Major sleep medicine organizations, including the American Academy of Sleep Medicine, have called for eliminating seasonal clock changes. Their preferred option is permanent standard time, because it more closely matches the body's natural light-dark cycle.

Researchers have linked the spring shift, when we lose an hour, to short-term disruptions such as less sleep and more daytime drowsiness. Some studies have also found small, temporary increases in heart attack and stroke risk in the days after the spring change. These findings describe averages across large populations, not a risk that every individual will experience, but they are a main reason health groups favor ending the switch.

## Safety and energy

The safety picture is mixed. Evening daylight can reduce some crimes and traffic collisions involving pedestrians at dusk. Darker winter mornings under permanent daylight time could raise risks for children walking to school and for early commuters. Research on crash rates after clock changes has also found short-lived spikes, especially after the spring change.

The original energy-saving argument is weaker than many assume. Modern studies generally find the effect on electricity use is small, and in some regions it is close to zero, because heating, cooling and electronics use have changed since the policy began.

## The economic argument

Business groups, retailers and the recreation and tourism sectors have often backed more evening daylight, arguing that people shop and spend more when it is light after work. Others point to costs from lost productivity after the spring change and from the confusion of coordinating schedules across time zones, especially in transportation, broadcasting and finance. Estimates of the economic effect vary a great deal depending on the method used, so they should be treated with caution.

## The lesson of the 1970s

The U.S. has tried this before. In 1974, Congress approved year-round daylight time as an energy-saving experiment. Public support dropped during the first dark winter mornings, and Congress repealed the measure the next year. That history is a major reason lawmakers and scientists urge care about which permanent time to choose.

## What to expect this November

For now, nothing changes in law. Sunrise and sunset will shift an hour earlier on November 1, and evenings will get dark sooner. Some practical steps can ease the adjustment:

- Shift bedtime 15 to 20 minutes earlier for a few nights beforehand.
- Get outdoor light in the morning after the change.
- Keep meal and wake-up times steady.
- Take extra care when driving at dusk, when drivers and pedestrians are adjusting to earlier darkness.

## The bottom line

Americans say in surveys that they want an end to clock changes, but they are less united on which time to keep. Until Congress picks one, and until states get the option or the mandate to act, the clocks will keep moving twice a year. Meanwhile, the evidence supports one clear conclusion: whichever time is chosen, staying on it all year is likely to be better than switching back and forth.

*This article is for general information and does not constitute medical advice. People with sleep or health concerns should speak with a qualified health professional.*

items.title: The Thanksgiving Table Bill: What Turkey, Stuffing and Pie Could Cost This Year
items.body:
With Thanksgiving about five weeks away, the cost of the holiday meal is already a popular topic at kitchen tables and in grocery aisles. Households that host a big dinner often start planning early, and many want to know whether the familiar menu of turkey, stuffing, vegetables and pie will cost more or less than last year.

This guide explains what tends to drive the price of the main ingredients and how to read the annual dinner-cost surveys without over-interpreting a single headline number. It does not predict exact prices. Costs vary by region, store and week.

## Why Thanksgiving Prices Get So Much Attention

Thanksgiving is one of the few meals in the United States built around a nearly standard menu. That makes it a convenient yardstick. Because most households buy a similar set of items, changes in the total are easy to compare from one year to the next. The meal also stands in for broader grocery inflation, so a rise or fall in the "dinner bill" often shapes conversations about everyday food costs.

## Turkey: Supply, Disease and Timing

The turkey is usually the most expensive single item, and its price depends on several factors:

- **Flock size.** Producers decide months ahead how many birds to raise. Outbreaks of avian influenza can shrink flocks and tighten supply, which has pushed turkey prices up in past years.
- **Feed and energy costs.** Grain prices, fuel and processing expenses all feed into the final shelf price.
- **Retail strategy.** Many grocery chains treat turkey as a "loss leader." They discount it heavily, sometimes in exchange for a minimum purchase, to bring shoppers into the store.
- **Timing.** Frozen turkeys are often cheapest in the weeks right before the holiday, while fresh birds usually cost more per pound.

## Dairy: Butter, Cream and Milk

Dairy shows up in mashed potatoes, casseroles, rolls and pie fillings. Prices follow milk supply, feed costs, seasonal demand and trade conditions. Butter and cream tend to be more volatile than milk, and demand rises sharply in the weeks around the holidays. Store brands are often noticeably cheaper than name brands for the same ingredient.

## Produce: Weather and Transportation

Fresh vegetables, cranberries, sweet potatoes and potatoes are sensitive to weather, harvest conditions and transportation costs. A poor growing season in one region can lift prices nationally, while a strong harvest can keep them steady. Canned and frozen versions of many items are often cheaper and last longer, which makes them a practical option for the side dishes.

## Stuffing, Rolls and Pie

Packaged stuffing mix, bread, flour, sugar and pie crusts depend largely on wheat, sugar and packaging costs. Pumpkin and pecan pie ingredients can swing with crop conditions. Many shoppers save money by baking from scratch, while others find a store-bought pie cheaper once their time and extra ingredients are counted.

## How to Read the Annual Dinner-Cost Surveys

Several organizations publish a yearly estimate of the cost of a Thanksgiving dinner. The best known is the American Farm Bureau Federation's survey, which prices a classic menu for a set number of guests, typically ten, using reports from volunteer shoppers across the country. Some retailers and consumer groups publish their own versions. A few points help put these numbers in context:

1. **Check the menu.** Surveys price a specific list of items. If your table has more dishes, different dishes or a larger crowd, your total will differ.
2. **Look at the method.** Some surveys use regular shelf prices, while others include promotions. Results can differ by several dollars for that reason alone.
3. **Compare like with like.** A survey from one organization is not directly comparable to a survey from another.
4. **Remember it's an average.** Prices in a big city, a rural town and a discount grocer can differ widely.
5. **Watch the trend, not the decimal.** A small change from last year may not mean much. A larger shift, and what caused it, is more informative.
6. **Note the timing.** Prices are collected weeks before the holiday, and store sales may change what you actually pay.

## Practical Ways to Keep the Bill in Check

- **Make a menu and a list first.** Planning cuts impulse purchases and food waste.
- **Compare unit prices.** The price per pound or per ounce shows the real value better than the sticker price.
- **Use store promotions and loyalty programs,** but check whether a turkey deal requires a minimum spend.
- **Consider alternatives.** A smaller bird, a turkey breast or a different main dish can lower costs for a smaller group.
- **Buy shelf-stable items early** and watch for sales on baking staples.
- **Share the load.** Asking guests to bring a side dish or dessert spreads out the expense.
- **Plan for leftovers** so less food goes to waste.

## The Bottom Line

Nobody can say exactly what your Thanksgiving table will cost until you are at the checkout. Still, understanding what moves the price of turkey, dairy and produce, and knowing how the annual surveys are built, can help you separate real trends from headlines. A little planning and some comparison shopping will usually do more for your budget than any national average.

*This article is for general information only and is not financial advice. Prices vary by location and retailer.*

items.title: [Logistics 101 #14] The 98% Trap: Why "Almost On Time" Costs You Real Money
items.body:
> A supply chain you can't measure is one you can't defend — this lesson covers the KPIs that matter, the SCOR framework that organizes them, how to price risk before it hits, and why emissions are becoming a logistics metric too.

## Today's Concept

Every warehouse manager will tell you things are "running fine." The job of performance measurement is to replace that sentence with a number.

**Start with KPIs — but the right ones.** The single most useful logistics metric is the **perfect order rate**: the share of orders delivered on time, complete, undamaged, and with correct paperwork. It's brutal because it multiplies:

```
Perfect order rate = on-time % x complete % x damage-free % x correct-docs %
0.98 x 0.98 x 0.98 x 0.98 = 0.922
```

Four "excellent" 98% scores produce a 92% perfect order rate. Eight orders in every hundred go wrong somewhere. That gap between component metrics and end-to-end metrics is where most supply chain complaints live.

Other core measures:

- **Order fulfillment cycle time** — order placed to customer receipt.
- **Cash-to-cash cycle time** — days between paying your supplier and getting paid by your customer: `inventory days + receivable days - payable days`.
- **Inventory turns** and **days of supply** — how hard your working capital is working.
- **Cost to serve** — total logistics cost per order, per unit, or per customer.

**SCOR gives these a home.** The Supply Chain Operations Reference model, maintained by ASCM, is the industry's standard vocabulary. Classic SCOR organizes a supply chain into six process areas — Plan, Source, Make, Deliver, Return, and Enable — and scores them on five attributes: reliability, responsiveness, agility, cost, and asset management efficiency. The current digital revision (SCOR DS) renames and regroups those processes and folds in environmental and social measures alongside the economic ones. The details shift between versions; the useful idea doesn't. SCOR forces you to say *which attribute* you're optimizing, because you cannot maximize all five. Faster response usually costs more. Lower cost usually means less agility. Pick, then measure.

**Risk management is measurement pointed at the future.** The standard move is a risk register: list what could break, score each item on **likelihood** and **impact**, and multiply to rank. But logistics risk has a twist — the worst events are the low-probability ones, so probability estimates are close to worthless. A more practical pair of questions, popularized by MIT's David Simchi-Levi:

- **Time to Recover (TTR):** if this node goes dark, how long until supply is restored?
- **Time to Survive (TTS):** how long can we keep serving customers on inventory and alternatives?

If TTR exceeds TTS, you have a real exposure, whatever the probability. The fixes are familiar: dual sourcing, safety stock at the right node, qualified backup carriers, postponement (finish the product late, closer to demand), and visibility into tier-2 and tier-3 suppliers — because the plant that shuts down is usually one your buyer has never heard of.

**Sustainability is now a logistics KPI, not a press release.** Transportation and purchased goods sit in **Scope 3** emissions, which for most retailers and manufacturers dwarf their own facilities and fleet. The operational levers are the same ones that cut cost: raise trailer load factor, cut **empty miles**, shift long hauls from truck to intermodal rail, right-size packaging, consolidate LTL shipments into full truckloads. Emissions per ton-mile is the metric; the EPA's SmartWay program is the common US benchmark for carrier performance.

## In Everyday Life

Say you run a Columbus, Ohio distributor selling houseware to a big-box retailer. Your goods move from a supplier in Vietnam, through the Port of Long Beach, by rail to Chicago, then by truck to your DC.

Your internal dashboard looks great: 97% on-time from the DC, 99% pick accuracy. Then your retail customer's scorecard arrives. Large chains run **OTIF (on-time, in-full)** programs and charge suppliers for misses — Walmart's has assessed fees of roughly 3% of the value of noncompliant goods. On $8 million of annual shipments to that account, a 10% miss rate is about $24,000 in fines, plus expedited freight to chase the shortfalls, plus a worse position in next year's negotiation.

Then the port slows down for three weeks. You dig into your risk register and find the honest numbers: TTR for that ocean lane is 5 weeks; your TTS on current inventory is 3 weeks. Two weeks exposed. The options each carry a price you can actually compute — air freight a partial order at maybe $4–6 per kilogram versus roughly $0.30 by ocean, hold four extra weeks of safety stock at a carrying cost of 20–25% of inventory value per year, or qualify a second supplier at a few months of engineering time.

None of those choices is obvious. But once you've written down the perfect order rate, the fine schedule, TTR versus TTS, and the carrying cost, you're making a business decision instead of a guess.

## Three-Line Recap

1. Component metrics lie; end-to-end metrics like perfect order rate and cash-to-cash tell the truth, because errors multiply rather than average.
2. SCOR provides shared language and forces the trade-off — reliability, responsiveness, agility, cost, and assets cannot all be maximized at once.
3. Manage risk by comparing time-to-recover with time-to-survive rather than guessing probabilities, and treat emissions per ton-mile as a real KPI alongside cost.

## ✅ Self-Quiz

**1.** A shipper hits 99% on-time, 98% complete, 99% damage-free, and 100% correct documentation. What is the perfect order rate?
  A) 99.0%  B) 98.0%  C) about 96.0%  D) 100%

**2. (O/X)** A disruption with very low probability can safely be ignored in a risk register.

**3.** Cash-to-cash cycle time is calculated as:
  A) inventory days + receivable days − payable days
  B) receivable days + payable days − inventory days
  C) order cycle time + transit time
  D) revenue ÷ average inventory

## 📚 Today's Terms

- **Perfect Order Rate** — Share of orders delivered on time, complete, undamaged, and correctly documented; the four rates multiply.
- **SCOR** — The Supply Chain Operations Reference model, an ASCM-maintained standard for describing supply chain processes and scoring their performance.
- **Cash-to-Cash Cycle Time** — Days of working capital tied up between paying suppliers and collecting from customers.
- **TTR / TTS** — Time to Recover from a disrupted node versus Time to Survive on existing inventory; exposure exists when TTR is longer than TTS.
- **Scope 3 Emissions** — Indirect emissions from purchased goods and outsourced transportation, typically the largest share of a shipper's carbon footprint.

---

*Answers: 1 — C. 0.99 x 0.98 x 0.99 x 1.00 = 0.960, about 96%; four strong scores still leave four bad orders per hundred. 2 — X. Rank by impact as well as likelihood; low-probability, high-impact events are exactly the ones that require a survival plan, since probability estimates for rare events are unreliable. 3 — A. Inventory days plus receivable days minus payable days; paying suppliers later and collecting sooner shortens the cycle.*
